title: The Age of the Sphinx
yt_title: Is the Sphinx Older Than the Pharaohs? The Evidence
verdict_scope: a Sphinx carved thousands of years before the pharaohs (Schoch's first carving at about 7000 to 5000 BCE, or about 12,000 years ago in Schoch and Bauval 2017): Awaiting evidence, the Shorts' grade, reached again from the evidence. Its only support is one reading of the weathering of the pit walls and floor, which salt, damp sand and the fast decay of these soft beds can also explain (Gauri et al. 1995; Harrell 1994), while the quarry sequence (the trench cut after Khafre's causeway, its blocks in temples built after the Valley Temple's granite), the builders' debris, the light dates of the Sphinx Temple and the absence of any earlier workplace all point to the pyramid age. Not Ruled out, because the carving itself has never been dated directly. Graded separately in the weighing: carved from the living rock, its quarry feeding the temple, Established; carved in Khafre's building works around 2500 BCE, Strong evidence (Khufu or Djedefre would shift it by decades); a start a few centuries earlier (Reader), Open question.
hook: Was the Sphinx carved before the pharaohs?
end_line: Old when a prince dreamed in its shadow. Older still? Only a date can tell.
structure_note: chapters[0] is the cold open and the title beat (no chapter card; YouTube chapter 0:00). Chapters 1 to 5 are the story chapters; 'The weighing' carries the verdict, the test and the close. Shot ids s1..sN are in story order; 'alias of sN' means a return to that panel.

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:hushed wonder, painting it]A lion as long as a jumbo ^jet, with the face of a ^king, lying in a pit at the edge of the ^desert@noun. [act:the reveal, slower][tune:fall]Nobody built it from ^blocks: it was carved out of the hill ^itself.

[d:tension][act:storytelling, intrigued]Around {1400|fourteen hundred} BCE, a young prince fell asleep in its ^shadow. [act:quieter, the dream]In his dream, the lion asked him to clear away the ^sand, and promised him a ^crown. [p:0.93][act:the turn, slower][tune:fall]Even then, it was more than a thousand years ^old.
[d:wonder][act:the child's question, wide-eyed][tune:rise]So how old is the Great ^Sphinx, really? [act:leaning in, the bigger question][tune:rise]Was it carved long before the ^*pharaohs*?

shots.say: A lion as long as a jumbo jet, with the face of a king, lying in a pit at the edge of the desert. Nobody built it from blocks: it was carved out of the hill itself.
shots.draw: HERO IMAGE, fully drawn from the first frame: dawn sky, the Great Sphinx in profile (head to the left, east), 73 m long and 20 m high at about 15 units a metre: striped nemes headdress, the lappet behind the face, the worn face with no nose, the forepaws stretched out, the long back, the haunch and the curled tail; its body banded in soft and hard layers; behind it the far wall of its pit and, beyond, Khafre's pyramid with its cap of casing. A person (1.7 m) at the paws. On 'jumbo jet' a dashed outline of a 747 (about 71 m) draws over the body, label '73 m'; on 'carved out of the hill' the layers of the pit wall light up and continue straight through the lion's body.

shots.say: Around 1400 BCE, a young prince fell asleep in its shadow. In his dream, the lion asked him to clear away the sand, and promised him a crown. Even then, it was more than a thousand years old.
shots.draw: Night: the Sphinx buried to its shoulders in drifted sand, moon above; a small sleeping figure in its shadow (chip 'about 1400 BCE'); on 'dream' a dotted line rises from him to a pale double crown that glows; on 'more than a thousand years', a strip along the bottom: 'carved, about 2500 BCE' to 'the dream, about 1400 BCE', bracket '1,100 years'.

shots.say: So how old is the Great Sphinx, really? Was it carved long before the pharaohs?
shots.draw: Back to the hero panel (alias of s1), wide: a lilac dotted arrow sweeps from the Sphinx far to the left into the dawn sky, past a few faint date ticks, and a large lilac '?' pops on 'pharaohs'.

lines: [d:calm][act:warm, setting out]The age of the ^Sphinx. [act:the promise, friendly][tune:fall]What the rock, the rain and the builders' ^rubbish can tell us.

shots.say: The age of the Sphinx. What the rock, the rain and the builders' rubbish can tell us.
shots.draw: intro_title card 'The Age of the Sphinx' over the dimmed s3 panel. Nothing else drawn.

lines: [d:calm][act:setting the scene, unhurried]Giza, on the west bank of the ^Nile, beside modern ^Cairo. [act:a little wonder, the deep past]About fifty million years ago, all of this lay under a warm, shallow ^sea.
[act:explaining, vivid]Its limestone is packed with fossil shells shaped like little ^coins.
[d:aside][act:dry, amused]The Greek geographer ^Strabo was told they were the builders' ^lentils, turned to stone. [act:the punchline, deadpan][tune:fall]He thought that not ^improbable.

shots.say: Giza, on the west bank of the Nile, beside modern Cairo. About fifty million years ago, all of this lay under a warm, shallow sea.
shots.draw: Map View(30.6, 31.9, 29.6, 30.4): the Nile and its valley, pins 'Giza' (gold) and 'Cairo'; scale bar 10 km. On 'fifty million years ago' a translucent blue sea floods the whole map from the north, label 'a shallow sea, about 50 million years ago'.

shots.say: Its limestone is packed with fossil shells shaped like little coins. The Greek geographer Strabo was told they were the builders' lentils, turned to stone. He thought that not improbable.
shots.draw: Close-up on a limestone face lit from the side: dozens of disc-shaped fossil shells (nummulites), a few broken open to show their spiral; a coin pops beside one for size (label 'fossil shells'). On 'Strabo', a small bowl of lentils pops at right with a dotted lilac link to the discs (label 'the builders' lentils?'), tag 'Strabo, about 2,000 years ago'.

lines: [d:build][p:0.93][act:explaining, a picture]The rock lies in layers, like a ^cake. [act:counting them off][tune:level]At the bottom, the hard rock of an old ^reef. [act:same pace][tune:level]Above it, bands of soft and hard ^stone. [act:the last one][tune:fall]And on top, a harder, better ^stone.

[act:the method, clear]The carvers didn't stack ^stones. [act:the picture, vivid]They dug a deep trench in the shape of a ^U around a block of bedrock, and shaped what was ^left: [act:the reveal, delighted][tune:fall]the reef for the floor, the soft bands for the ^body, the better stone for the ^head.

shots.say: The rock lies in layers, like a cake. At the bottom, the hard rock of an old reef. Above it, bands of soft and hard stone. And on top, a harder, better stone.
shots.draw: A section through the plateau's bedrock, three units building in from the bottom as named: a knobbly reef ('old reef'), alternating soft and hard bands ('soft and hard bands'), a pale top layer ('better stone'); beside it a small layer cake with the same three layers.

shots.say: The carvers didn't stack stones. They dug a deep trench in the shape of a U around a block of bedrock, and shaped what was left: the reef for the floor, the soft bands for the body, the better stone for the head.
shots.draw: Left, a plan from above: a U-shaped trench (dark) cut round a rectangle of bedrock, open to the east. Right, the same layered section: the trench cuts down both sides of a central block, then the lion's outline draws on the block, its head in the top layer, its body in the bands, its base on the reef; three short leaders 'head', 'body', 'floor'.

lines: [d:reveal][act:the twist, intrigued]And the stone they dug out didn't go to ^waste. [p:0.93][act:the size, a touch of awe]Blocks of up to a hundred ^tonnes were dragged a short way east, to build a ^temple in front of the lion.

[d:build][act:the question, curious][tune:rise]How do we ^know? [act:explaining, step by step]In {1980|nineteen eighty}, the geologist Thomas ^Aigner logged every layer in the trench, and each of the {173|hundred and seventy-three} big blocks in the ^temple. [p:0.93][act:the reveal, delighted]Most of those blocks carry a yellow ^band: the same band that runs across the lion's chest and ^shoulders. [act:the analogy, light][tune:fall]Like slices of a layer cake, fitted back onto the ^cake.

shots.say: And the stone they dug out didn't go to waste. Blocks of up to a hundred tonnes were dragged a short way east, to build a temple in front of the lion.
shots.draw: Side view at dawn: the trench beside the Sphinx; big blocks rise out of the trench one by one and slide east (left) on sledges hauled by tiny teams, stacking into the walls of a temple in front of the paws; label 'up to 100 tonnes' on the biggest block.

shots.say: How do we know? In 1980, the geologist Thomas Aigner logged every layer in the trench, and each of the 173 big blocks in the temple.
shots.draw: A geologist's log: left, a column of the trench layers with small fossil icons (urchin, oyster, shark's tooth, coral); right, 173 small block icons pop in a grid as he counts (label '173 blocks'), each getting a tick; tag 'Aigner, 1980'.

shots.say: Most of those blocks carry a yellow band: the same band that runs across the lion's chest and shoulders. Like slices of a layer cake, fitted back onto the cake.
shots.draw: The Sphinx in profile at left with a yellow band glowing across its chest and shoulders; at right the temple wall's blocks, most crossed by the same yellow band; dashed gold links join the bands. On 'layer cake' a cake slice slides back into its gap in a small cake.

lines: [d:aside][act:the landing, warm][tune:fall]So the Sphinx isn't a ^building. [act:a smile, the image][tune:fall]It's what the quarrymen left ^standing.

shots.say: So the Sphinx isn't a building. It's what the quarrymen left standing.
shots.draw: The Sphinx in its trench, three-quarter light: the stone that was cut away floats above and around it as faint dashed block outlines, which drift east towards the temple; the lion alone stays solid.

lines: [d:calm][act:orienting, clear]Around {2500|twenty-five hundred} BCE, Khufu's son ^Khafre built the second great pyramid at ^Giza. [act:the plan, unhurried]From its temple, a causeway runs almost half a kilometre down to a second temple, by the valley ^floor.
[act:pointing, a little wonder][tune:fall]And right beside that lower temple, at the foot of the causeway, lies the ^Sphinx.

shots.say: Around 2500 BCE, Khufu's son Khafre built the second great pyramid at Giza. From its temple, a causeway runs almost half a kilometre down to a second temple, by the valley floor.
shots.draw: Plan of the Giza plateau, north up (positions after published plans): the three pyramids as squares, Khafre's lit; chip 'about 2500 BCE'; his pyramid temple, then the causeway draws itself down to the Valley Temple (label 'almost half a kilometre', scale bar 100 m).

shots.say: And right beside that lower temple, at the foot of the causeway, lies the Sphinx.
shots.draw: Same plan (alias of s13), the camera closer on the foot of the causeway: the Sphinx in its trench glows beside the Valley Temple, with the Sphinx Temple in front of it.

lines: [d:build][act:the detective, curious][tune:level]But beside isn't the same as built ^together. [act:the first clue, clear]Look at the trench's south ^wall: it's the edge of Khafre's ^causeway. [p:0.93][act:the analogy, light]When a flowerbed follows the exact edge of a path, the path was there ^first. [act:the payoff][tune:fall]So the trench was cut after the causeway was ^built.

[act:the second clue, steady]Next door, the Valley Temple's granite was already in place when the Sphinx Temple's wall went up against ^it. [act:the third, crisp][tune:fall]And both temples are built alike: giant limestone blocks, cased in red ^granite.

shots.say: But beside isn't the same as built together. Look at the trench's south wall: it's the edge of Khafre's causeway. When a flowerbed follows the exact edge of a path, the path was there first. So the trench was cut after the causeway was built.
shots.draw: Close plan of the trench and the causeway: the trench's south wall and the causeway's north edge flash together as one line (label 'one edge'). Inset: a garden path and a flowerbed hugging its edge, tags '1 path' and '2 flowerbed'; then the same tags on the plan: '1 causeway', '2 trench'.

shots.say: Next door, the Valley Temple's granite was already in place when the Sphinx Temple's wall went up against it. And both temples are built alike: giant limestone blocks, cased in red granite.
shots.draw: Where the two temples meet, in section: a red granite block of the Valley Temple's bench, then the Sphinx Temple's huge limestone end block lowered over it (tags '1' and '2'). Then the two temples side by side in plan, limestone cores (tan) inside red granite casing, labels 'Valley Temple' and 'Sphinx Temple'.

lines: [d:reveal][act:the find, delighted]Then there's the ^rubbish. [p:0.93][act:storytelling, vivid]In {1978|nineteen seventy-eight}, in a corner of the trench, Zahi ^Hawass and Mark ^Lehner found big blocks abandoned on their way to the ^temple. [act:the details, savouring them]In a little heap of debris: half of an everyday jar from the pyramid ^age, and stone ^hammers, one still flecked with ^copper, as if from striking a ^chisel.

[d:build][act:the last clue, thoughtful]The job@work was never ^finished. [act:explaining, clear]The temple's blocks still carry rough ^knobs, and none of the hundreds of tombs of that age at Giza names a priest of the ^Sphinx. [act:the landing, quiet][tune:fall]A building site, abandoned in ^mid-stride.

shots.say: Then there's the rubbish. In 1978, in a corner of the trench, Zahi Hawass and Mark Lehner found big blocks abandoned on their way to the temple.
shots.draw: The trench's north-east corner seen from above and the side: three big blocks lie on a dragging track, short of the temple; two small excavators kneel by them; chip '1978'.

shots.say: In a little heap of debris: half of an everyday jar from the pyramid age, and stone hammers, one still flecked with copper, as if from striking a chisel.
shots.draw: A finds tray under a lamp: half of a plain jar (the broken edge shown), four round hammerstones; on 'copper' green-gold flecks glint on one stone's striking end; a dotted ghost copper chisel taps against it (label 'a chisel?').

shots.say: The job was never finished. The temple's blocks still carry rough knobs, and none of the hundreds of tombs of that age at Giza names a priest of the Sphinx. A building site, abandoned in mid-stride.
shots.draw: Left: the temple's corner blocks with rough bosses still sticking out (rings mark them, label 'never trimmed'). Right: a row of small tomb doorways with inscriptions; a magnifier passes along them, none lights (label 'no priest of the Sphinx').

lines: [d:aside][act:fair, even][tune:rise]Was it ^Khafre, then? [act:the mainstream, plain]Most Egyptologists think ^so. [act:fair, the minority][tune:level]A few credit his father, ^Khufu, or his brother, ^Djedefre. [act:the landing, a small smile][tune:fall]Either way, the answer moves by ^decades, not ^millennia.

shots.say: Was it Khafre, then? Most Egyptologists think so. A few credit his father, Khufu, or his brother, Djedefre. Either way, the answer moves by decades, not millennia.
shots.draw: A small family tree (Khufu above, Djedefre and Khafre below) beside a time axis from 3000 to 2400 BCE: their three reigns as short bars side by side, Khafre's bright ('most Egyptologists'); a bracket 'decades' spans the three; far left on the axis a long dim bar 'millennia' for scale.

lines: [d:calm][act:plain, a respectful introduction]Around {1990|nineteen ninety}, the Boston University geologist Robert ^Schoch read@past these walls ^differently. [act:describing, a careful eye]The soft layers are cut back into deep, rounded ^hollows, and long cracks run down from the ^top.

[act:sympathetic, his view]To him, that's the signature of ^rain, streaming down rock for thousands of ^years. [p:0.93][act:his logic, clear and fair]Wind@air carves level grooves; rain cuts ^down. [act:his comparison, intrigued]And tombs of Khafre's age nearby are so lightly worn, he says, you can still read@present their ^inscriptions.

shots.say: Around 1990, the Boston University geologist Robert Schoch read these walls differently. The soft layers are cut back into deep, rounded hollows, and long cracks run down from the top.
shots.draw: The trench wall face on, hard and soft beds; a small geologist with a hand lens at its foot (chip '1990'); on 'rounded hollows' the soft beds cut back into rolling recesses; on 'cracks' four deep vertical fissures draw down from the top.

shots.say: To him, that's the signature of rain, streaming down rock for thousands of years. Wind carves level grooves; rain cuts down. And tombs of Khafre's age nearby are so lightly worn, he says, you can still read their inscriptions.
shots.draw: Rain streams down the wall and into the fissures (blue). Two small swatches: 'wind' (sharp level grooves, arrows sideways) and 'rain' (rounded, cut downwards, arrows down). Then a tomb front with a crisp carved inscription pops at right (label 'tomb of Khafre's age').

lines: [d:build][act:the test, building]In {1991|nineteen ninety-one}, he and the geophysicist Thomas ^Dobecki sent sound waves into the floor of the ^pit. [p:0.93][act:the analogy, clear]Weathering creeps into rock like damp into a ^wall: the longer it's open to the air, the deeper it ^goes.
[p:0.9][act:the result, precise]In front and along the sides, the floor was weathered up to two and a half metres ^deep. [act:same, precise][tune:fall]Behind the lion, only a little over ^one.

[d:build][act:his reasoning, fair]Schoch reasoned that the back was cut free later, under ^Khafre, and the front long ^before. [p:0.9][act:stating his date, even]In {1992|nineteen ninety-two}, he put the first carving between seven thousand and five thousand ^BCE. [act:the bigger claim, eyebrows up]In a {2017|twenty seventeen} book with Robert ^Bauval, he went further: about twelve thousand years ^ago.

shots.say: In 1991, he and the geophysicist Thomas Dobecki sent sound waves into the floor of the pit. Weathering creeps into rock like damp into a wall: the longer it's open to the air, the deeper it goes.
shots.draw: Section through the pit's floor: a hammer strikes a plate, a row of geophones, sound arcs spread and echoes return (chip '1991'). Inset: a house wall with damp creeping up from the floor, tide marks for '1 year' and '10 years'.

shots.say: In front and along the sides, the floor was weathered up to two and a half metres deep. Behind the lion, only a little over one.
shots.draw: Plan of the Sphinx in its pit, from above: a weathered band in the floor drawn thick in front and along both sides (label 'up to 2.5 m deep') and thin behind the haunches (label 'about 1.2 m'); beside it two depth bars with a person (1.7 m) for scale.

shots.say: Schoch reasoned that the back was cut free later, under Khafre, and the front long before. In 1992, he put the first carving between seven thousand and five thousand BCE. In a 2017 book with Robert Bauval, he went further: about twelve thousand years ago.
shots.draw: Timeline from 12,000 BCE to 1 CE: Khafre's mark about 2500 BCE (amber), tag 'the back'; Schoch's blue dashed band 7000 to 5000 BCE (tag '1992', 'the front'); then a lilac dotted mark near 10,000 BCE (tag '2017, with Bauval: about 12,000 years ago').

lines: [d:build][act:more evidence, steady]He sees the same story in the ^temples: their limestone cores, he argues, were already weathered when the granite facing was ^added. [act:the last clue, intrigued]And the head looks too ^small for the body, as if it had been recarved from an older ^one.

shots.say: He sees the same story in the temples: their limestone cores, he argues, were already weathered when the granite facing was added.
shots.draw: A temple wall in section: a limestone core block with a rounded, worn face; a red granite facing slab moves in and its back follows the worn curve; tag 'worn first?' in blue dashes.

shots.say: And the head looks too small for the body, as if it had been recarved from an older one.
shots.draw: The Sphinx in profile; the head outlined in gold; a larger, dotted lilac head outline (an older head, as he suggests) behind it; a bar compares head and body lengths, label 'too small?'.

lines: [d:aside][act:fair, even-handed]Not every geologist who sees water goes so ^far. [act:introducing him, respectful]Colin ^Reader reads the damage as rain ^runoff, pouring off the plateau into the ^pit. [act:landing his view][tune:fall]His Sphinx is older than ^Khafre, but by a few ^centuries, not thousands of ^years.

shots.say: Not every geologist who sees water goes so far. Colin Reader reads the damage as rain runoff, pouring off the plateau into the pit. His Sphinx is older than Khafre, but by a few centuries, not thousands of years.
shots.draw: The plateau in section sloping east down to the pit: rain falls far upslope and blue runoff arrows run down the surface and pour over the pit's edge (label 'runoff'). A small timeline: Khafre's mark, Reader's short green band just before it ('a few centuries'), Schoch's blue band far to the left, dimmed.

lines: [d:aside][act:the landing, thoughtful][tune:fall]For Schoch, the walls are a ^clock. [act:the question, quiet][tune:rise]The question is whether that clock keeps good ^time.

shots.say: For Schoch, the walls are a clock. The question is whether that clock keeps good time.
shots.draw: The worn wall again (alias of s21), wider: a clock face draws itself on the rock, its hands turning unevenly, fast then slow; a lilac '?' beside it.

lines: [d:calm][act:the other side, crisp]Other geologists ^answered, starting with the same ^walls. [p:0.93][act:explaining, step by step]Lal ^Gauri's team found ^salt in the soft layers. [act:the mechanism, vivid]Night dew soaks in; by day it dries, and salt crystals grow in the pores and burst the ^grains, [act:the analogy, homely][tune:fall]like the white crust that flakes a damp cellar ^wall.

[act:simple, matter of fact]Soft bands crumble back, hard ones ^stay: rounded hollows, no rain ^needed. [p:0.93][act:the surprise, delighted]The long cracks, they argue, are natural joints, widened by groundwater long before there were ^humans.

shots.say: Lal Gauri's team found salt in the soft layers. Night dew soaks in; by day it dries, and salt crystals grow in the pores and burst the grains, like the white crust that flakes a damp cellar wall.
shots.draw: Magnified grains of a soft bed: a moon, dew drops soak in (blue); a sun, the water dries and white salt crystals grow between the grains, pushing them apart (small cracks). Inset: a cellar wall with a white crust flaking off.

shots.say: Soft bands crumble back, hard ones stay: rounded hollows, no rain needed. The long cracks, they argue, are natural joints, widened by groundwater long before there were humans.
shots.draw: The wall: the soft bands retreat into rounded hollows while the hard ones stay sharp, no rain drawn. Then a deep section of the limestone: joints widen into blue channels as groundwater moves; a time arrow 'millions of years ago' to 'humans', a tiny person at its far end.

lines: [d:build][act:a second answer, steady]James ^Harrell adds the ^sand. [act:explaining, a picture]For long stretches, the pit was full of it, wetted by rain and by Nile ^floods. [act:the logic, clear][tune:fall]Damp sand, pressed against soft rock for centuries, eats it ^away.

[d:build][p:0.93][act:the speed, pointed]And this rock decays ^fast. [act:counting, firm][tune:level]By the prince's dream, the body was already so worn it needed a new skin of ^stone. [act:same rhythm][tune:level]In {1988|nineteen eighty-eight}, a chunk of its shoulder ^fell. [act:the image, quiet][tune:fall]On windy days, flakes peel off the walls while you ^watch.

shots.say: James Harrell adds the sand. For long stretches, the pit was full of it, wetted by rain and by Nile floods. Damp sand, pressed against soft rock for centuries, eats it away.
shots.draw: Side section: the pit filled with sand up to the lion's neck; a damp blue zone spreads through the lower sand; at left a blue flood line rises to just below the pit floor (label 'Nile floods'); small arrows of moisture press into the walls.

shots.say: And this rock decays fast. By the prince's dream, the body was already so worn it needed a new skin of stone. In 1988, a chunk of its shoulder fell. On windy days, flakes peel off the walls while you watch.
shots.draw: The Sphinx in profile: casing blocks pop along its worn body (chip 'about 1400 BCE'); then a chunk drops from the shoulder (chip '1988'); then wind lines and small flakes peeling off the pit wall behind.

lines: [d:build][act:fair, the climate][tune:level]Rain hadn't ended, ^either: even Reader finds runoff at Giza after Khafre's ^time. [act:the critics, crisp][tune:level]The weak layer under the floor may simply be softer rock, laid down that ^way. [act:same, plain][tune:level]The temple's limestone looks trimmed to fit its granite, not worn ^before it. [act:the last, light][tune:fall]And to Lehner, the odd part is the body, not the head: stretched, perhaps, to get past a great natural ^crack.

shots.say: Rain hadn't ended, either: even Reader finds runoff at Giza after Khafre's time.
shots.draw: A strip of time from 3000 to 2300 BCE: Khafre's mark; rain bars keep falling after it (label 'runoff after Khafre').

shots.say: The weak layer under the floor may simply be softer rock, laid down that way. The temple's limestone looks trimmed to fit its granite, not worn before it. And to Lehner, the odd part is the body, not the head: stretched, perhaps, to get past a great natural crack.
shots.draw: Three small panes: the pit floor's weak layer relabelled 'softer rock?'; the granite and limestone joint where a chisel trims the limestone to the granite's rough back (arrow reversed from s26); the Sphinx's body with a natural crack across its back and a bracket 'one head length' along the body.

lines: [d:reveal][act:turning the page, curious][tune:rise]And the ^archaeology? [p:0.93][act:the big gap, slower]Around seven thousand BCE, Egypt had no farming villages at ^all. [act:explaining, vivid]The first farmers we know of turn up around {5400|fifty-four hundred} BCE, by a lake in the ^Fayum, storing grain in pits lined with ^baskets. [act:the question, pointed][tune:rise]So who carved a seventy-three-metre lion, long before ^them?

[d:build][act:fair, his answer]Schoch points to Göbekli ^Tepe, in Turkey, where hunter-gatherers raised carved pillars around {9500|ninety-five hundred} ^BCE. [act:fair, weighing it]True, and ^remarkable. [p:0.93][act:the difference, clear]But they left a ^trail: thousands of grinding stones, flint tools, animal ^bones. [act:the point, quiet][tune:fall]At Giza, nobody has found a workplace from that ^age.

shots.say: And the archaeology? Around seven thousand BCE, Egypt had no farming villages at all. The first farmers we know of turn up around 5400 BCE, by a lake in the Fayum, storing grain in pits lined with baskets. So who carved a seventy-three-metre lion, long before them?
shots.draw: Map of northern Egypt: the Nile, Giza, the Fayum lake (pin 'Fayum'); a time strip 7000 to 5000 BCE with an empty stretch ('no farming villages') then a tag 'first farmers, about 5400 BCE'; a grain pit in section, lined with basketry, full of grain; on 'who carved', the Sphinx's silhouette in lilac dots over 7000 BCE with a '?'.

shots.say: Schoch points to Göbekli Tepe, in Turkey, where hunter-gatherers raised carved pillars around 9500 BCE. True, and remarkable. But they left a trail: thousands of grinding stones, flint tools, animal bones. At Giza, nobody has found a workplace from that age.
shots.draw: Two columns under one band 'about 9500 to 5000 BCE': left 'Göbekli Tepe', a carved T-pillar standing on a layer that fills with grinding stones, flints and bones as named; right 'Giza', the same layer empty, a lilac dashed outline and a small '?' (label 'nothing found').

lines: [d:build][act:a new clock, curious]And one clock can be read@present ^directly. [p:0.93][act:the analogy, gentle]Sunlight wipes a stone's surface clean, like a ^blackboard; [act:same, gentle]in the dark, natural radiation slowly writes on it ^again. [act:the payoff][tune:fall]Measure the writing, and you know when it last saw the ^sun.

[p:0.93][act:the result, precise]In {2015|twenty fifteen}, four stones of the Sphinx Temple were read@past this ^way: between about thirty-one hundred and twelve hundred ^BCE, with wide ^margins. [act:the landing, quiet][tune:fall]None came near the age of the first ^farmers.

shots.say: And one clock can be read directly. Sunlight wipes a stone's surface clean, like a blackboard; in the dark, natural radiation slowly writes on it again. Measure the writing, and you know when it last saw the sun.
shots.draw: A blackboard: a sun's rays wipe it clean; then darkness falls and tally marks appear one by one (label 'natural radiation'); beside it a temple block being set in a wall, its hidden face lit by the same tally marks.

shots.say: In 2015, four stones of the Sphinx Temple were read this way: between about thirty-one hundred and twelve hundred BCE, with wide margins. None came near the age of the first farmers.
shots.draw: Timeline 8000 BCE to 1 CE: four dots with error bars (3100 +/- 540, 2740 +/- 640, 2220 +/- 220, 1190 +/- 340 BCE) pop; Khafre's mark; 'first farmers, about 5400 BCE' and Schoch's dimmed band far to the left; a bracket shows the gap.

Where drills went down, including groundwater test holes around 2009, one angled under the left paw, cameras found only natural rock and cracks. Whether any crossed the hollow picked up in 1991, no report says.

shots.say: So, let's weigh it. Carved from the living rock, its quarry feeding the temple in front: established. Carved in Khafre's building works, around 2500 BCE: strong evidence. Khufu or Djedefre would shift that by decades.
shots.draw: A four-row ledger fills row by row, each with a pictogram and a grade chip that pops as the grade is said: 'cut from the rock, quarry to temple' Established; 'Khafre's works, about 2500 BCE' Strong evidence (small tag 'Khufu or Djedefre: decades').

shots.say: Its case rests on one reading of the weathering, which salt, damp sand and fast decay can also explain. And every trace we can date points to the pyramid age. The walls really are deeply worn. But rock that crumbles at its own pace makes a poor clock.

[act:building][tune:level]More light dates, from the quarry's own ^surfaces. [act:building][tune:level]A camp of that age nearby, with an earlier crew's hearths and ^tools. shots.say: What would change our minds? Something datable, sealed under the oldest weathering in the pit: charcoal, a tool, a pot, older than the pharaohs. More light dates, from the quarry's own surfaces. A camp of that age nearby, with an earlier crew's hearths and tools. And for the hollow under the paws: one drill aimed at it, and the survey data out in the open.
shots.draw: Four 'wanted' items in lilac dashed outline, popping as named: charcoal, a tool and a pot under a weathered crust ('sealed and datable'); a stone face with a light-dating sample ('more light dates'); a hearth with tools ('a camp of that age'); a narrow drill aimed at the hollow and an open data file ('one drill hole, open data').

shots.say: It was already old when a prince dreamed in its shadow. Whether it's older still, only a date can tell. Weigh it yourself.
shots.draw: The opening Sphinx (alias of s1) at dusk, wide and quiet; a faint lilac '?' far to the left in the sky. Then the end card (verdict chip 'Awaiting evidence').

description:
A lion as long as a jumbo jet, carved out of the bedrock at Giza and worn into deep hollows. Was it carved long before the pharaohs, as the geologist Robert Schoch reads its weathering, or by Khafre's workmen around 2500 BCE?

We follow the rock from a fifty-million-year-old sea floor to the quarry that made both the lion and its temple, weigh the rain hypothesis at its strongest against salt, damp sand and the builders' own rubbish, read the Dream Stele of Thutmose IV, and end on the tests that would change the verdict. Verdict: a Sphinx thousands of years older than the pharaohs is Awaiting evidence; carved in Khafre's building works, Strong evidence.

facts_added.fact: The Sphinx is carved from the Mokattam Formation, Eocene limestone about 50 million years old, laid down where an ancient sea left a lagoon with shoals and coral reef.
facts_added.source: AERA, Geology of the Sphinx (Lehner)

facts_added.fact: Three members: Member I, the hard, brittle rock of an ancient reef, forms the base (rising to about 12 ft at the rump and 2 to 3 ft at the paws); Member II, layers alternating softer and harder, forms most of the body; Member III, softer at the neck and harder at the head, good building stone, forms the head.
facts_added.source: AERA, Geology of the Sphinx; Gauri 1984, ARCE Newsletter 127 (Member II about 10 m thick, beds 1 to 2 m)

facts_added.fact: Strabo describes chips 'like lentils in both form and size' in the heaps in front of the pyramids, said to be the petrified leftovers of the workmen's food, which he thought 'not improbable' (these are nummulite fossils).
facts_added.source: Strabo, Geography 17.1.34

facts_added.fact: The builders quarried a U-shaped ditch out of the natural limestone, leaving a core that they sculpted as the Sphinx; the ditch opens east to a terrace.
facts_added.source: Lehner 1992, Cambridge Archaeological Journal, doi:10.1017/S0959774300000421; Lehner 2003

facts_added.fact: In 1980 Thomas Aigner, a geologist from the University of Tubingen, studied the layers of the Sphinx, its ditch and each of the 173 core blocks of the Sphinx Temple, using their fossils; the layers run continuously through adjacent blocks.
facts_added.source: Lehner 2003, The Sphinx, in Hawass (ed.), The Treasures of the Pyramids

facts_added.fact: Blocks from the upper layers (at head level and possibly higher) went into Khafre's Valley Temple; as the ditch deepened, blocks were dragged directly east to build the Sphinx Temple; most of these carry a yellow band like the layers at the Sphinx's chest and shoulder height; blocks weigh up to 100 tons.
facts_added.source: Lehner 2003

facts_added.fact: Khafre built the second pyramid at Giza around 2500 BCE; he was Khufu's son.
facts_added.source: Lehner 2003; Lehner & Hawass 2017

facts_added.fact: Khafre's causeway is about 494.6 m long, from his pyramid temple down to the Valley Temple; the Sphinx sits at its valley end.
facts_added.source: Pyramid of Khafre survey figure (Wikipedia); Lehner 1992

facts_added.fact: The south side of the Sphinx quarry is the north side of the foundation of Khafre's causeway, so the causeway precedes the quarry in the construction sequence.
facts_added.source: AERA, Khafre's Monuments

facts_added.fact: Ricke recognised that the builders had completed the granite bench, and probably the whole granite casing, of the Valley Temple before building the Sphinx Temple's wall of large limestone blocks, whose end block fits over a granite block of that bench.
facts_added.source: Lehner 2003 (after Ricke)

facts_added.fact: The Sphinx Temple's masonry, multi-toned limestone core blocks with granite casing, matches Khafre's Valley Temple; the two stand on the same terrace.
facts_added.source: Lehner 1992

facts_added.fact: In 1978 Zahi Hawass and Mark Lehner found blocks abandoned in a corner of the quarry while being dragged to build the Sphinx Temple; a small mound of debris in the north-east corner of the ditch held half of a common Fourth Dynasty jar and hammer stones, one with copper flecks on its striking end.
facts_added.source: Hadingham 2010, Smithsonian Magazine; Lehner 2003; AERA, Khafre's Monuments (blocks intended for the third course)

facts_added.fact: The Sphinx Temple was left unfinished (extra stock left on its huge corner core blocks), and no titles of priests or priestesses of the Sphinx are known from the hundreds of Old Kingdom tombs at Giza.
facts_added.source: Lehner 2003; AERA, Khafre's Monuments

facts_added.fact: Some Egyptologists credit Khufu (the face is compared with his only known statuette) or Djedefre (who ruled briefly and was buried at Abu Roash); Lehner judges Khafre the most probable owner.
facts_added.source: AERA, Khafre's Monuments

facts_added.fact: Schoch began his Sphinx work around 1990; he read the rounded, rolling profile and the vertical fissures of the enclosure walls as precipitation weathering, and noted that Fourth Dynasty tombs nearby are so little weathered that their inscriptions can still be read.
facts_added.source: Schoch 1992, KMT 3(2); Schoch 1995, Habibi 14(2)

facts_added.fact: The 1991 seismic survey (Dobecki and Schoch) found the floor of the enclosure weathered up to 6 to 8 ft (about 1.8 to 2.4 m) deep in front and along the sides, but about 4 ft (about 1.2 m) behind the Sphinx; the abstract states that subsurface weathering is not uniform and reports cavities flanking the Sphinx and between its paws.
facts_added.source: Schoch 1995, Habibi 14(2); Dobecki & Schoch 1992, Geoarchaeology, doi:10.1002/gea.3340070603

facts_added.fact: Schoch held that Khafre had the back of the Sphinx carved free from the cliff, and from 50 to 100 percent deeper weathering in front estimated the initial carving at about 7000 to 5000 BCE; he also argued that the temples' limestone cores weathered before their granite facing was added and that the head is too small for the body.
facts_added.source: Schoch 1995, Habibi 14(2); Schoch 1992, KMT 3(2)

facts_added.fact: In 2017 Schoch and Robert Bauval argued that the Sphinx was first built by a pre-pharaonic civilisation about 12,000 years ago, contemporaneous with Gobekli Tepe.
facts_added.source: Schoch & Bauval 2017, Origins of the Sphinx (Inner Traditions), publisher's description

facts_added.fact: Reader reads the uneven erosion as rainfall runoff rather than direct rainfall, documents runoff at Giza through the late Fifth Dynasty, and suggests the Sphinx may predate Khufu (a few centuries, not thousands of years).
facts_added.source: Reader 2001, Archaeometry, doi:10.1111/1475-4754.00009; Bordeau summary in Hall of Maat (as used in LF.01)

facts_added.fact: Gauri and colleagues showed that weathering in an arid climate can produce the rounded profile and that the channels in the walls are pre-Pliocene karst features formed by underground water; the salts in the beds are gypsum and halite.
facts_added.source: Gauri, Sinai & Bandyopadhyay 1995, Geoarchaeology, doi:10.1002/gea.3340100203; Gauri 1984

facts_added.fact: Harrell argues that sand filling the enclosure, periodically wetted by Nile floods and rain, weathered the soft beds; that the seismic low-velocity layer may reflect the rock's original character rather than weathering; and that the limestone was cut to fit the irregular backs of the granite, not the reverse; the 4,500 years since Khafre are enough.
facts_added.source: Harrell 1994, KMT 5(2): 70-74; Harrell 1994, KMT 5(3): 3-4

facts_added.fact: Thutmose IV (about 1401 BCE) covered the eroded body with large limestone casing slabs and built mud-brick walls more than eight metres tall around the ditch, 'like a giant cartouche'; later repairs date to the 26th Dynasty and to Greek and Roman times.
facts_added.source: Lehner 2003; Lehner 1992

facts_added.fact: In the 1980s two sizeable stones fell: masonry veneer from the left hind paw in 1981 and a large piece of bedrock from the right shoulder in 1988; on windy days flakes of limestone blow off the quarry walls; the 1990s restoration lasted a decade.
facts_added.source: AERA, Geology of the Sphinx

facts_added.fact: The earliest domesticated plants and animals in the Fayum date from about 5400 BC (Merimde from about 4900 BC); the Fayum sites show hearths and basket-lined granaries with emmer and barley.
facts_added.source: Linseele et al. 2014, PLOS ONE, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0108517

facts_added.fact: Gobekli Tepe (about 9500 to 8000 BCE) has yielded more than 7,000 food-processing artefacts, flint tools and the bones of hunted animals.
facts_added.source: Dietrich L. et al. 2019, PLOS ONE, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0215214; Dietrich O. et al. 2012, Antiquity, doi:10.1017/S0003598X00047840

facts_added.fact: Surface luminescence dates for Sphinx Temple stones: 2220 +/- 220 BC (limestone), 2740 +/- 640, 3100 +/- 540 and 1190 +/- 340 BC (granite); the authors say none of the dates for the Sphinx Temple or Giza corroborates a prehistoric age, though a pre-Khafre date cannot be ruled out.
facts_added.source: Liritzis & Vafiadou 2015, Journal of Cultural Heritage, doi:10.1016/j.culher.2014.05.007

facts_added.fact: The Dream Stele: granite, about 3.6 m tall and 15 tons, set between the paws in year 1 of Thutmose IV (about 1401 BCE); in the dream the god asks to be saved from the sand and promises the kingship; it is a reused lintel from a doorway of one of Khafre's temples.
facts_added.source: Lehner 2003; Mallet 1888, Records of the Past n.s. 2 (translation); Dream Stele dimensions as given by Lehner and standard references

facts_added.fact: Nineteenth-century copies of the stele show part of Khafre's name in its damaged middle; that part has since flaked off (gone by the re-excavation of the 1920s).
facts_added.source: Mallet 1888 (Khafri named in the damaged middle); Colavito 2001 on Henry Salt's 1820 copy; Hassan 1953 as summarised in standard references

facts_added.fact: In spring 1978 an SRI team drilled five four-inch holes on the strongest resistivity and seismic anomalies (three in the temple area, two in the bedrock floor); a borehole television camera showed only minor natural cracks.
facts_added.source: Dolphin 1999, Geophysical studies around the Sphinx

facts_added.fact: The 1991 seismic anomalies under the Sphinx's front lay in front of the front left paw; in 1997 Hawass said that permission would not be given to drill into the Sphinx on the basis of anomalies, conservation being the priority.
facts_added.source: Lehner & Hawass 1997, NOVA Online, Pyramids: The Inside Story (PBS); Dobecki & Schoch 1992, Geoarchaeology, doi:10.1002/gea.3340070603

facts_added.fact: Around 2008 to 2009 Cairo University's Engineering Center drilled groundwater test holes into the bedrock of the Sphinx enclosure for the antiquities authority (four holes 20 m deep with cameras lowered, one bored beside the left paw at an angle under the monument); the water table lay about 15 ft beneath the statue and pumps were installed; the report states that no tunnels or rooms were found. No report I found says whether any hole crossed the 1991 anomaly.
facts_added.source: Hadingham 2010, Saving the Sphinx, NOVA (PBS); Heritage Key 2011, Drilling Under the Sphinx (video report)

facts_added.fact: Lehner reads the head as a reserved block about 20 by 20 royal cubits and the body as about one head-length too long, perhaps extended to get past the major fissure that cuts through all layers.
facts_added.source: Lehner 1992; Lehner 2003

facts_added.fact: Arithmetic for the pictures: 73 m of Sphinx against a Boeing 747-400 of about 71 m; 6 to 8 ft = 1.8 to 2.4 m, said 'up to two and a half metres'; 4 ft = 1.2 m, said 'a little over one'; 2500 BCE to 1400 BCE = 1,100 years.
facts_added.source: Arithmetic on the cited figures
